quests.instruction: Write the capital letter L. It is a corner: one line down, one line across.
quests.question: L
quests.hint: Start at the top and pull straight down. Without lifting, turn the corner and slide right along the bottom line.
quests.explanation: L is made from a vertical stroke and a horizontal stroke, the two lines you practiced in the first levels. The bottom stroke should be shorter than the tall one.
quests.funFact: The Phoenician letter that became L was called 'lamed', which is thought to mean 'ox goad', a pointed stick used to guide oxen.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter I with a small bar at the top and at the bottom.
quests.question: I
quests.hint: Draw a short bar across the top, pull a line down from its middle, then add a short bar across the bottom.
quests.explanation: The bars on I are called serifs. They make the letter easy to tell apart from a plain standing line or a lowercase l.
quests.funFact: English is unusual in always writing the word 'I' with a capital letter.

quests.instruction: Write I and L side by side. Keep both exactly the same height.
quests.question: I L
quests.hint: Make I first. Then look at where its top and bottom are, and match them when you write L.
quests.explanation: Capital letters should all reach the same height so they look like a neat row of soldiers.
quests.funFact: The shapes of our capital letters come from letters the Romans carved into stone monuments.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter T: a roof across the top, and a post standing in its middle.
quests.question: T
quests.hint: Draw the top bar from left to right. Then start at its middle and pull a line straight down.
quests.explanation: T begins with a horizontal stroke and finishes with a vertical one. The post should start at the center of the bar so the letter looks balanced.
quests.funFact: The Phoenician letter that became T was called 'taw', which meant 'mark' or 'sign'.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter H: two standing lines joined by a bridge in the middle.
quests.question: H
quests.hint: Pull down on the left, then pull down on the right. Join them with a short line across the middle.
quests.explanation: H is two vertical lines and a horizontal bar. Putting the bar halfway up keeps the letter balanced, with both sides the same.
quests.funFact: H is often silent in English, in words such as 'hour' and 'honest'.

quests.instruction: Write T and H next to each other. Make the tops line up.
quests.question: T H
quests.hint: Think about the top line of the page. The top bar of T and the tops of H should both touch it.
quests.explanation: Keeping tops level is called alignment. Even two letters look much tidier when they share the same top and bottom.
quests.funFact: The pair of letters 'th' is one of the most common in English.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter E: one line down, then three bars pointing right.
quests.question: E
quests.hint: Pull down first. Then, starting from the line each time, add the top bar, the middle bar (a little shorter), and the bottom bar.
quests.explanation: E has one vertical stroke and three horizontal strokes. Every bar starts at the stem, and the middle one is shortest so the letter looks tidy.
quests.funFact: A novel called 'Gadsby', published in 1939, runs to about 50,000 words without using the letter E once.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter F. It looks like E but has no bottom bar.
quests.question: F
quests.hint: Pull down, add the top bar, then add a shorter bar in the middle. Leave the bottom bare.
quests.explanation: F is E with its last bar taken away. Noticing which part is missing is how you tell similar letters apart.
quests.funFact: F, U, V, W and Y all grew from the same Phoenician letter, called 'waw'.

quests.instruction: Write E and F one after the other. Check that the bottom is different.
quests.question: E F
quests.hint: Write E with three bars, then F with two. Say 'three, two' as you draw.
quests.explanation: E and F share the same stem and top bar, so counting the bars is how your hand remembers which is which.
quests.funFact: Dictionaries list words in alphabetical order so you can find them quickly.

quests.instruction: From memory, write the three letters L, I and T in a row.
quests.question: L I T
quests.hint: Picture each one before you write it: L is a corner, I has two small bars, T is a roof with a post.
quests.explanation: Recalling letters without looking helps your memory more than copying does. If one was tricky, trace it again later.
quests.funFact: The word 'alphabet' comes from the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta.

quests.instruction: Write the letter with three bars first, then the one with two bars.
quests.question: E F
quests.hint: The letter with three bars is E, and F has two. Start each with the line going down.
quests.explanation: Describing a letter by its parts is a clever memory trick. 'Stem plus bars' lets you rebuild a letter whenever you need it.
quests.funFact: Capital letters are also called uppercase because printers once kept them in the upper drawer of a case of metal type.

quests.instruction: Write H, E, F and T in a row. Keep equal gaps and equal heights.
quests.question: H E F T
quests.hint: Leave a gap about as wide as a finger between each letter, and check that all the tops line up.
quests.explanation: A row of letters needs two things: the same height and even gaps. This is your first practice at writing a line of text.
quests.funFact: The oldest known alphabets were first used about 3,800 years ago in the Middle East.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter V: slant down to a point, then slant up.
quests.question: V
quests.hint: Start at the top left and go down to the bottom point. Without lifting, go up to the top right.
quests.explanation: V is two slants that meet at a point on the baseline. Both slants should be the same length so the V looks balanced.
quests.funFact: U and V used to be the same letter. English began to separate them only a few hundred years ago.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter W: slant down, up, down, up, like two V's joined together.
quests.question: W
quests.hint: Start at the top left. Slant down to the baseline, up to the middle, down again, then up to the top right. Count four slants.
quests.explanation: W is four slants forming two valleys. Counting the strokes helps you slow down at each turn.
quests.funFact: The name of W is 'double u', because it was once written as two U's or V's side by side.

quests.instruction: Write V and W together and notice how W is wider.
quests.question: V W
quests.hint: Write V first. Then write W a little wider so each of its two valleys is about as big as one V.
quests.explanation: Comparing similar shapes teaches you how many strokes each one needs and how wide it is.
quests.funFact: In Roman numerals V stands for 5 and X for 10.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter X: two slanted lines crossing in the middle.
quests.question: X
quests.hint: Slant down from top left to bottom right. Lift, then slant down from top right to bottom left. Cross in the middle.
quests.explanation: X is made of two diagonals that cross at the center. Putting the crossing in the middle makes it look even on all sides.
quests.funFact: People have used an X to mean 'wrong', 'kiss' or 'mark the spot', which makes it one of the most flexible letters.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter Y: two short slants that meet, and a post going down.
quests.question: Y
quests.hint: Slant down from top left to the middle. Slant down from the top right to meet it, then pull straight down to the baseline.
quests.explanation: Y uses two slants that join and a vertical stem. Where the slants meet should be halfway down, not at the very top.
quests.funFact: The letter Y can act like a consonant in 'yes' and like a vowel in 'my'.

quests.instruction: Write X and Y one after the other. Match their heights.
quests.question: X Y
quests.hint: Both letters reach the top line and the baseline. Check the tops and bottoms after you write them.
quests.explanation: Crossing slants and meeting slants look different but must be the same height to sit neatly together.
quests.funFact: Doctors, scientists and puzzle makers use X and Y as names for unknown things, from number puzzles to graphs.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter Z: a line across the top, a slant down, and a line across the bottom.
quests.question: Z
quests.hint: Draw across the top from left to right. Slant down to the bottom left, then draw across the bottom to the right.
quests.explanation: Z has two flat lines connected by one diagonal. The slant goes the opposite way from the stroke you use for A's right side.
quests.funFact: In the United States the last letter is called 'zee', but in Britain, Australia and many other countries it is called 'zed'.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter A: two slants that meet at the top, then a bar across the middle.
quests.question: A
quests.hint: Slant up to the point, then slant down on the other side. Lift your pen and add a short bar about halfway up.
quests.explanation: A is built from the roof shape you drew earlier plus a crossbar. The bar needs to be level and lower than the middle of the letter.
quests.funFact: The letter A began as a picture of an ox's head, and turned upside down to the shape we know today.

quests.instruction: Write A and Z together, then say them aloud: first letter and last letter.
quests.question: A Z
quests.hint: Write A with its roof and bar, leave a gap, then write Z. Make them the same height.
quests.explanation: Writing the first and last letters together gives you a good picture of the alphabet's start and end.
quests.funFact: The English alphabet has 26 letters.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter K: a standing line, then two slants that touch it in the middle.
quests.question: K
quests.hint: Pull down first. Then, starting at the top right, slant in until you touch the line in the middle, and slant back out to the bottom right.
quests.explanation: K combines a vertical stroke and two diagonal strokes that meet at one point. If the slants meet at the right spot, the letter looks balanced.
quests.funFact: The Phoenician letter that became K was called 'kaph', which is thought to mean 'palm of the hand'.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter M: two standing lines with a V shape between them.
quests.question: M
quests.hint: Pull down on the left. Slant down to the baseline in the middle, slant up to the top, then pull straight down on the right.
quests.explanation: M has four strokes: two verticals and two slants. The middle point should reach the baseline, so the letter holds its shape.
quests.funFact: The letter M is thought to come from an old symbol for water, with wavy lines.

quests.instruction: Write K and M one after the other. Check where the strokes meet.
quests.question: K M
quests.hint: For K, the slants meet the stem halfway down. For M, the slants meet the baseline. Keep the letters the same height.
quests.explanation: Both letters have pointed meeting places, but at different heights. Noticing where lines meet is a handwriting skill.
quests.funFact: The letters M and N are called nasal sounds, because air flows through your nose when you say them.

quests.instruction: Write the capital letter N: a line down, a slant down, then a line up.
quests.question: N
quests.hint: Pull down on the left. Go back to the top and slant down to the bottom right, then pull straight up on the right.
quests.explanation: N has two verticals joined by one diagonal. Starting the diagonal at the top-left corner makes it run corner to corner.
quests.funFact: The Phoenician letter that became N was called 'nun', thought to mean 'fish'.

quests.instruction: Write Z, Y and X, which are the last three letters, in backwards order.
quests.question: Z Y X
quests.hint: Say them aloud as you write: Z, Y, X. Make each one reach the same height.
quests.explanation: Writing in reverse alphabetical order pushes you to recall each letter's shape instead of the order you automatically recite it.
quests.funFact: Z is among the least used letters in English.

quests.instruction: Write K, M, N and X in a row. Space them evenly.
quests.question: K M N X
quests.hint: After each letter, leave a gap as wide as your fingertip. Check that all four letters are the same height.
quests.explanation: These letters all use diagonals, and writing four in a row builds the endurance you need for words.
quests.funFact: The first printed books were made in the 1400s, and each letter was a small piece of metal that had to be placed by hand.

quests.instruction: From memory, write the three letters F, H and K.
quests.question: F H K
quests.hint: Think of them as stem letters: all three start with a line going down. F adds bars, H joins two stems, K adds slants.
quests.explanation: Grouping letters by their first stroke helps you remember them. These three all start with a downward line.
quests.funFact: A pangram is a sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet, such as 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog'.

quests.instruction: Write M, N, W and V in a row. Notice which ones go up and down.
quests.question: M N W V
quests.hint: M and N have two standing lines, and W and V are all slants. Take your time at the pointed corners.
quests.explanation: These four letters all zigzag. Controlling the pointed corners is the main challenge of this group.
quests.funFact: The capital letter W looks like an upside-down M.

quests.instruction: Write T, Y, Z and E. Each has a flat bar on top or bottom.
quests.question: T Y Z E
quests.hint: Look for the flat bars before you write: T and Z have a top bar, and E has bars across the top, middle and bottom. Y has no flat bar, so double-check it.
quests.explanation: Describing letters by shapes helps recall. Notice how T and Z both begin with the same top line.
quests.funFact: Writers have used the same 26 letters to create millions of different books.
